items.t: Practice makes perfect.
items.d: Things get easier the more you try them.

items.t: Look before you leap.
items.d: Think about what could happen before you act.

items.t: Two heads are better than one.
items.d: A friend might spot an answer you missed.

items.t: Many hands make light work.
items.d: Tidying a room is easier when everyone helps.

items.t: Better late than never.
items.d: You can still make a start, even if you meant to start sooner.

items.t: Don't count your chickens before they hatch.
items.d: Wait to see what happens before you count on it.

items.t: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
items.d: Keep another plan ready in case your first one fails.

items.t: Actions speak louder than words.
items.d: Helping someone means more than just saying you will.

items.t: Every cloud has a silver lining.
items.d: Even a hard day can hold something good.

items.t: A stitch in time saves nine.
items.d: Fix a small tear now, before it gets bigger.

items.t: Haste makes waste.
items.d: When you rush, mistakes can make you do the job twice.

items.t: Out of sight, out of mind.
items.d: It's easy to forget things you don't see often.

items.t: Easy come, easy go.
items.d: Things gained quickly can disappear quickly, too.

items.t: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
items.d: A shared job can get messy when everyone tries to be in charge.

items.t: All that glitters is not gold.
items.d: Something can look fine without being as good as it seems.

items.t: Gravity pulls things toward Earth.
items.d: When you drop a sock, gravity pulls it to the floor.

items.t: Friction can slow things that slide.
items.d: A book pushed across a table slows down as it rubs against the table.

items.t: Moving things tend to keep moving.
items.d: When the car stops, your seat belt stops you from moving forward.

items.t: The same push speeds up a light cart more than a heavy cart.
items.d: With an equal push, an empty shopping cart speeds up faster than a full one.

items.t: A push is met by an equal push in the other direction.
items.d: Push water backward with your hands as you swim. The water pushes you forward.

items.t: Light bounces off a mirror.
items.d: When you brush your teeth, light from your face bounces off the mirror into your eyes.

items.t: Light can bend when it goes from water into air.
items.d: A straw in a clear glass of water can look bent at the water line.

items.t: Sounds start with something shaking back and forth.
items.d: Pluck a guitar string and watch it shake as it makes a sound.

items.t: Faster shaking makes a higher note.
items.d: On a guitar, pressing a string closer to the bridge leaves less string to shake and makes a higher note.

items.t: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.
items.d: A metal spoon warms up when you leave it in hot soup.

items.t: Water pushes upward on things in it.
items.d: A beach ball pops up when you let it go underwater.

items.t: A push farther from a pivot can turn something more easily.
items.d: A door swings open more easily when you push near the handle than when you push near the hinges.

items.t: Two north poles of magnets push each other away.
items.d: Bring the north ends of two toy bar magnets together and feel them push apart.

items.t: Electric current needs a complete path to keep flowing in a simple circuit.
items.d: A flashlight switch breaks the path when you turn it off.

items.t: Rubbing materials together can build up an electric charge.
items.d: Rub a balloon on your hair. The balloon can then pull your hair toward it.

items.t: To triple a number, add three copies of it.
items.d: Triple 7 is 7 + 7 + 7 = 21.

items.t: Adding two odd numbers gives an even number.
items.d: 5 + 7 = 12. You can split 12 into two equal groups of 6.

items.t: Swap the numbers you multiply and the answer stays the same.
items.d: 3 rows of 4 dots make 12 dots. Turn the page sideways and you get 4 rows of 3, still 12.

items.t: To multiply by 9, multiply by 10 and take away one copy.
To multiply a whole number by 5, multiply by 10 and halve the result.
items.d: For 5 × 14, first find 10 × 14 = 140. Half of 140 is 70.

items.t: A whole number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3.
items.d: For 42, add 4 + 2 = 6. Since 6 is a multiple of 3, 42 divides by 3 exactly. 42 ÷ 3 = 14.

items.t: Fractions stay equal when you multiply the top and bottom by the same nonzero number.
items.d: Multiply the 1 and 2 in 1/2 by 3. You get 3/6, which is still half.

items.t: To find a quarter of something, divide it into four equal parts.
items.d: A quarter of 20 grapes is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 grapes.

items.t: A rectangle's area is its length times its width.
items.d: A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has area 6 × 4 = 24 square centimeters.

items.t: For a shape with straight sides, add the side lengths to find the distance around it.
items.d: A rectangle with sides 8 cm and 3 cm is 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22 cm around.

items.t: The three angles of a triangle on flat paper always add up to 180°.
items.d: With angles of 90° and 35°, the last angle is 180° - 90° - 35° = 55°.

items.t: A circle's diameter is twice its radius.
items.d: If it's 4 cm from the center to the edge, it's 2 × 4 = 8 cm all the way across the center.

items.t: A prime number has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
items.d: Only 1 and 7 divide 7 with no leftover, so 7 is prime.

items.t: An average is the amount everyone would get if the total were shared equally.
items.d: Three friends have 2, 4 and 9 stickers. That's 15 stickers, so the average is 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

items.t: To find 10 percent of a number, divide it by 10.
items.d: 10 percent of 80 is 80 ÷ 10 = 8.

items.t: Penguins use their wings like flippers.
items.d: They flap them underwater to swim after food.

items.t: American flamingos get their pink color from their food.
items.d: Tiny algae and small animals they eat contain pigments, which give their feathers color.

items.t: Bats are the only mammals that can fly by flapping their wings.
items.d: Flying squirrels glide, like a paper plane.

items.t: Dolphins come to the surface for air.
items.d: They breathe through a blowhole on top of the head.

items.t: Male humpback whales sing long songs.
items.d: Their songs repeat groups of sounds and can be heard underwater.

items.t: An elephant uses its trunk to pick up food.
items.d: Its trunk is a long nose that can grab a meal and carry it to its mouth.

items.t: A butterfly starts life as an egg.
items.d: It hatches as a caterpillar, then changes inside a chrysalis before coming out as a butterfly.

items.t: Spiders have eight legs. Insects have six.
items.d: A ladybug may look a bit like a tiny spider, but it has six legs.

items.t: Female sea turtles lay their eggs on land.
items.d: They dig a nest in the sand and cover the eggs before going back to sea.

items.t: A kangaroo joey finishes much of its early growth in a pouch.
items.d: The newborn climbs into its mother's pouch, where it drinks milk.

items.t: Crocodiles lay eggs and can guard their nests.
items.d: A mother crocodile may even carry her hatchlings to water in her mouth.

items.t: Beavers build dams from sticks, mud and other things they find.
items.d: A dam slows a stream and can make a pond behind it.

items.t: An ostrich can run fast, but it cannot fly.
items.d: It has long, strong legs that help it take big steps.

items.t: A male seahorse carries the young before they are born.
items.d: The female puts her eggs into a pouch on the male. The young grow there until he gives birth.

items.t: Polar bears have black skin under their fur.
items.d: Their fur looks white, which helps them blend in with snow and ice.

items.t: The Sun is a star.
items.d: It looks much bigger than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: In empty space, light travels about 300,000 kilometers in one second.

items.t: Earth takes about a year to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth spins as it travels, so different places get daylight at different times.

items.t: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight.
items.d: As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunny side.

items.t: The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around Earth.
items.d: That is why we see nearly the same side of the Moon from Earth all the time.

items.t: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks some of the Sun's light from reaching Earth.
items.d: People in the Moon's shadow can see the Sun partly or fully covered.

items.t: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
items.d: It takes about 88 Earth days to go around the Sun once.

items.t: Venus takes longer to spin once than it takes to go around the Sun.
items.d: One spin takes about 243 Earth days. One trip around the Sun takes about 225.

items.t: Mars owes much of its red color to rusty dust.
items.d: Some of the iron in its rocks and dust has reacted with oxygen, like rust on an old bike.

items.t: Mars has two small moons.
items.d: Their names are Phobos and Deimos.

items.t: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system.
items.d: The Great Red Spot you can see in pictures of Jupiter is a huge storm.

items.t: Saturn's rings are made mostly of pieces of ice.
items.d: The pieces stay in motion, circling Saturn.

items.t: Uranus spins almost on its side.
items.d: Picture a spinning top that keeps spinning while tipped almost all the way over.

items.t: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to circle the Sun.
items.d: It is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.

items.t: We live in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
items.d: A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

items.t: Your smallest bones are inside your ears.
items.d: These tiny bones help pass vibrations from your eardrum to the inner ear.

items.t: Your pupil is the opening in the middle of your eye.
items.d: It usually gets bigger in dim light to let more light in.

items.t: Your heart is a pump made of muscle.
items.d: Every beat pushes blood through your body.

items.t: When you breathe in, oxygen from the air can pass into your blood.
items.d: It passes through the walls of tiny air sacs in your lungs.

items.t: Your tongue and nose work together when you taste food.
items.d: When you have a stuffy nose, food may seem to have less flavor.

items.t: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth.
items.d: It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

items.t: The Pacific Ocean is Earth's largest ocean.
items.d: It lies between Asia and Australia on one side and the Americas on the other.

items.t: The South Pole sits in Antarctica.
items.d: At the South Pole, a thick sheet of ice covers the land.

items.t: A map scale helps you work out real distances.
items.d: If 1 centimeter on a map stands for 1 kilometer, 3 centimeters stand for 3 kilometers.

items.t: An island is a piece of land surrounded by water.
items.d: An island can sit in a lake or river as well as in the ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: nocturnal.
items.d: A nocturnal animal is active at night. A barn owl often hunts after dark.

items.t: Word of the day: peninsula.
items.d: A peninsula is land with water around most of it. Much of Florida sits between the Gulf and the Atlantic Ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: palindrome.
items.d: A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Try it with the word level.

items.t: Word of the day: transparent.
items.d: If something is transparent, you can see clearly through it, like through clean window glass.

items.t: Word of the day: migrate.
items.d: To migrate is to move from one place to another. Many birds do this as the seasons change.
